lessons.title: Homer & the Epic Tradition
lessons.description: Who Homer was, oral epic poetry, and the Odyssey's place at the start of Greek literature.
lessons.content_html:
Who Was Homer?

The Odyssey is one of the oldest surviving works of Western literature, and tradition attributes it to a poet called Homer. Ancient writers generally believed Homer was a blind bard from Ionia — the western coast of what is now Turkey — who composed both the Iliad and the Odyssey. Modern scholars, however, debate whether a single poet called Homer ever existed, whether the two epics were composed by the same person, and whether the poems we have today were the work of one genius or the result of centuries of collaborative oral tradition. What matters for the exam is understanding the nature of the tradition that produced these poems.

The ancient Greeks themselves held Homer in extraordinary esteem. They called him simply “the Poet,” as though no other poet needed naming. His works were the foundation of Greek education: schoolchildren learnt passages by heart, rhapsodes (professional reciters) performed them at festivals, and philosophers quoted them to settle arguments about ethics and the gods.

Key Fact

The Odyssey was composed and performed in an oral tradition. The performer — a bard or rhapsode — used a stock repertoire of formulae, repeated phrases and set-piece scenes to compose the poem in performance, rather than reading from a written text.

What Makes the Odyssey an Epic?

An epic poem is a long narrative poem that deals with heroes and their deeds on a grand scale. The Odyssey has several defining features that mark it out as epic. It is composed in dactylic hexameter, the traditional metre of Greek epic — a rolling, stately rhythm that feels weightier than ordinary speech. It opens with an invocation of the Muse, asking the goddess of poetry to inspire the telling: the poem begins by asking the Muse to tell of “the man of many ways” — Odysseus. This signals immediately that the story is not merely entertainment but a divinely inspired account of great deeds.

Another epic convention is beginning in medias res — that is, starting the story in the middle of the action rather than at the beginning. When the Odyssey opens, Odysseus has already been wandering for ten years. We learn the earlier stages of his journey through his own narration to the Phaeacians in Books 9 and 10. This technique creates dramatic suspense and allows Homer to concentrate on the most significant episodes.

Three key oral-formulaic techniques appear throughout the Odyssey. First, epithets are fixed labels attached to characters: Odysseus is repeatedly called “resourceful Odysseus,” “godlike Odysseus,” or “the great tactician.” The rosy-fingered Dawn appears at the start of many mornings. These tags are not decorative accidents — they serve a practical function, allowing the performer to fill a particular part of the line while also reinforcing a character’s defining quality.

Second, formulae are repeated phrases used to describe recurring actions — drinking, eating, praying, greeting a guest. When Odysseus arrives at a new palace, Homer uses a set sequence of reception scenes that mirrors the rules of xenia. Third, Homeric similes — also called extended similes — pause the action to compare events to scenes from everyday life. When Odysseus finally kills the leading suitor, Homer compares the fallen man to an acrobat tumbling off a stool. These similes are vivid, surprising and ground the heroic world in the real world of the audience.

The Structure of the Odyssey

The Odyssey is divided into 24 books. The first four books follow Odysseus’s son Telemachus as he searches for news of his father — a section often called the Telemachy. Books 5–8 introduce Odysseus, stranded on the island of Calypso and eventually reaching the Phaeacians. Books 9–12 are Odysseus’s own first-person account of his adventures — a story within the story. Books 13–24 describe his return to Ithaca, his disguise as a beggar, the recognition scenes and the final bloody revenge on the suitors.

This structure is highly crafted. By placing Books 9–12 as a first-person flashback told by Odysseus to the Phaeacians, Homer allows the hero to be his own storyteller — which itself reveals something important about his character. Odysseus is a man of words as much as of deeds, and his ability to tell a compelling story is part of what makes him a great hero.

Key Fact

The Odyssey consists of 24 books. The prescribed books for study are Books 9, 10, 19, 21 and 22. Book 9 contains the Cyclops episode; Book 10 the encounter with Circe; Book 19 the recognition of Odysseus by his nurse Eurycleia; Book 21 the contest of the bow; and Book 22 the slaughter of the suitors.

A common misconception is that oral poetry must be imprecise or low quality. In fact, the scholarship of Milman Parry and Albert Lord in the 20th century showed that oral poets in the Balkans could compose thousands of lines of technically accomplished verse in performance. The repetitions, formulae and epithets in Homer are not signs of laziness — they are the tools of a sophisticated oral craft. The question of when the poems were written down is separate from the question of when they were first composed: the standard scholarly view is that the poems reached roughly their current form around the 8th century BC, and were written down during the 6th or 7th century BC.

It is also a misconception to think of Homer’s poems as simple myths invented for entertainment. The Greeks regarded them as a record of a real heroic age, a time when great men interacted directly with the gods. Modern archaeology has confirmed that a wealthy Bronze Age civilisation — the Mycenaean world — did exist, though the poems blend historical memory with legend and imagination in ways we cannot fully separate.

Themes and the Odyssey’s Appeal

The Odyssey is built around a series of powerful, interlocking themes. Nostos — the desire to return home — drives every choice Odysseus makes. The poem asks: what is it that makes a place “home”? Is it a physical location, a wife and son, a kingdom, or an identity? Every obstacle Odysseus faces tests whether his longing for Ithaca is stronger than the temptations placed in his way.

The tension between civilised and barbaric behaviour runs through the poem. Every new land Odysseus visits is measured against Greek standards of civilised life: do they practise xenia? Do they have proper laws and agriculture? The Cyclops Polyphemus fails every test. Circe begins as a monster but comes to embody a kind of civilised hospitality. These contrasts are not just entertaining — they define the civilised world that Odysseus is fighting to return to.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to ‘describe’ a feature of the Odyssey such as an epithet or a simile, give a specific example and explain what effect it creates — do not just define the term. The single biggest examiner concern is over-narration: students retelling what happens rather than analysing what Homer is doing and why. For an ‘explain’ question about oral composition, name the technique (epithet, formula, in medias res), give the specific example from the text, and say what purpose it serves for performer or audience. For essay questions, use named sources: quote the opening invocation, cite the specific books, and name the technical terms.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Odyssey is an oral epic attributed to Homer — composed in the oral tradition using epithets, formulae and extended similes, and structured to begin in medias res.
  • Epic conventions include the invocation of the Muse, dactylic hexameter, heroic subject matter and formal narrative scale; the five prescribed books (9, 10, 19, 21, 22) cover the adventures, the recognition and the revenge.
  • Central themes are nostos (the drive to return home), xenia (hospitality), and the contrast between civilised and barbaric behaviour — all of which are tested through Odysseus’s encounters on his journey.

practice_questions.text:
Read this paraphrase of the opening of the Odyssey:

'The poet asks his Muse to sing of the resourceful man who wandered many years after the fall of Troy, suffering greatly on sea and suffering greatly on land, as he struggled to save his own life and the lives of his companions. Yet for all his striving, he could not save them — they were destroyed by their own recklessness.'

What does this opening passage suggest about the way Homer presents Odysseus and his companions? Refer to specific details from the passage in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses at least two specific details from the passage with developed explanation of what they reveal about character or theme. Likely points: 'resourceful man' — the epithet immediately defines Odysseus by his intelligence and adaptability rather than strength; the contrast between Odysseus's survival and the crew's destruction establishes the theme of self-reliance; 'their own recklessness' — suggests the crew bear responsibility for their fate and signals the poem's interest in the theme of justice; the invocation of the Muse establishes epic authority and signals divine inspiration. Candidates who refer to specific words or phrases score more highly.
Secure: Two details identified and explained, without full analytical development.
Developing: One detail identified and explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the structure of the Odyssey — beginning in medias res — is effective for the audience.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the oral tradition is the most important feature for understanding Homer's Odyssey? Refer to a range of named sources and give a supported judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained argument that engages with both sides. For: oral composition explains epithets (e.g. 'resourceful Odysseus'), formulae (reception scenes, set-piece descriptions), extended similes and structural repetition; understanding the tradition helps us interpret the text as a performance rather than a fixed literary work; the invocation of the Muse signals the poem's oral origins. Against: the poem's thematic richness — nostos, xenia, justice, civilisation vs barbarism — is independent of its oral origins; the sophisticated in medias res structure and the nested narrative of Books 9–12 show literary artistry; the prescribed books reward close reading regardless of oral context. Top answers will name specific episodes and technical features, and reach a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Two points on each side with at least one named source.
Developing: Mostly one-sided with limited source use.
Emerging: General discussion, few named sources, no clear judgement.

glossary_terms.definition: The ancient Greek poet to whom the Iliad and the Odyssey are traditionally attributed; his identity as a single historical person remains debated.
A tradition in which poetry is composed and transmitted through spoken performance rather than writing, relying on stock phrases, standard scenes and the performer's memory.
A Greek professional singer who performed epic poetry from memory at festivals and public gatherings.
A long narrative poem on a grand scale, dealing with heroes, gods and momentous events, composed in formal verse and following traditional conventions.
A formal appeal to a divine being at the start of a poem, asking for inspiration and assistance in telling the story.
Latin for 'in the middle of things'; a narrative technique where the story begins at a late point in the action, with earlier events revealed through flashback.
A repeated descriptive phrase attached to a character or object in epic poetry, which fills a certain metrical slot in the line and acts as a shorthand identity tag.
An extended comparison in epic poetry that develops over several lines, comparing something in the main narrative to something from everyday life.
The craft of composing and delivering poetry in the oral tradition, using standard phrases, scenes and structural patterns to aid composition and memory.
The Greek concept of the longing or drive to return home, a central motivation for Odysseus throughout the poem.
The Greek code of hospitality, which required hosts to welcome strangers with food and shelter before asking their name or business, and guests to behave respectfully in return.

lessons.title: The Wanderings of Odysseus
lessons.description: Odysseus faces the Cyclops and Circe — cunning, danger and the temptations of the journey (Books 9–10).
lessons.content_html:
The Adventures of Book 9: Polyphemus the Cyclops

In Book 9, Odysseus narrates one of the most famous episodes in all of ancient literature: the encounter with the Cyclops Polyphemus. Odysseus and twelve chosen companions enter the enormous cave of Polyphemus — a giant with a single eye in the middle of his forehead — in hopes of receiving the gift of xenia, the code of hospitality that any Greek host owed a stranger. Instead, Polyphemus seals the cave with a massive boulder, seizes two of the men and eats them raw. He will do the same each morning and evening for as long as Odysseus remains his prisoner.

Odysseus’s first instinct is to stab Polyphemus in his sleep, but he quickly realises that would be fatal: only the giant can move the boulder that blocks the entrance. This moment shows the essential quality that distinguishes Odysseus from other heroes — his metis, or cunning intelligence. Brute force would kill him. He must think.

Key Fact

Odysseus’s escape plan has four stages: he finds a wooden stake in the cave, sharpens and hardens its tip in the fire, gets Polyphemus drunk on wine, blinds him by driving the stake into his eye, and then hides his men (and himself) beneath the giant’s rams as they leave the cave in the morning — since Polyphemus runs his hands over the backs of the sheep but does not check their undersides.

The ‘Nobody’ Trick

When Polyphemus, reeling from the wine, asks Odysseus his name so he can give him a “gift” of xenia in return, Odysseus tells him his name is “Nobody” — Outis in Greek. When Odysseus drives the stake into Polyphemus’s eye and the giant screams in agony, the neighbouring Cyclopes come to the entrance of the cave and ask what the matter is. “Nobody is killing me,” roars Polyphemus. The others conclude he must be ill and go away. The trick is a masterstroke of wordplay and deception: in the oblique grammatical forms Polyphemus uses when reporting his pain, mē tis (no one) becomes indistinguishable from mētis (cunning intelligence), creating a layered pun that quietly signals the quality that has defeated him.

However, Odysseus’s cunning is shadowed by a fatal flaw: excessive pride. As his ships pull safely away from the island, Odysseus cannot resist taunting Polyphemus and — crucially — revealing his real name. He shouts that it was Odysseus, son of Laertes, from Ithaca, who blinded him. Polyphemus calls on his father, the sea-god Poseidon, to curse Odysseus. This moment plants the seed of every subsequent delay in Odysseus’s return: Poseidon will make the sea his enemy for the rest of the poem.

Polyphemus embodies everything that is the opposite of civilised Greek society. He does not farm the land — he lives entirely off his flock. He has no concept of the gods or of xenia: when Odysseus invokes Zeus as the protector of guests, Polyphemus dismisses the gods entirely, saying the Cyclopes are stronger than any immortal. He lives alone, with no community or law. He eats his guests rather than feeding them.

Homer signals his barbarism through precise descriptive details. His cave is enormous but messy and unstructured — milk pails and cheese are stored without order; pens of lambs are organised only by age. He sits among his flocks like a man among animals. In contrast, Odysseus and his men, for all their fear, maintain their civilised behaviour, discussing options and following a plan. The contrast between Odysseus’s intelligence and the Cyclops’s brute size is the central drama of the episode.

Book 10: The Witch Circe

In Book 10, after further adventures, Odysseus’s ships arrive at the island of Aeaea, home of the goddess-witch Circe. Odysseus sends a scouting party — half his men — to explore the island. They find a palace in a woodland clearing, surrounded by wolves and lions, which are in fact men Circe has already transformed. Circe invites the men in and serves them a feast laced with a drug. When they eat, she strikes them with her wand and turns them into pigs. Only one man, Eurylochus, escapes because he hangs back, suspicious.

Odysseus sets out alone to rescue his men. On the way, the god Hermes meets him in the form of a young man and gives him the herb moly — a white flower with a black root — which will counteract Circe’s magic. He also instructs Odysseus to rush at Circe with his sword when she tries to transform him. Circe, astonished that her magic has failed, recognises Odysseus and surrenders. She restores his crew, and Odysseus and his men stay on the island for a year, feasting with Circe as their willing host.

Key Fact

Hermes gives Odysseus the herb moly to protect him from Circe’s magic. When Circe’s drug fails to transform Odysseus, she recognises him as the man foretold by Hermes. He forces her to swear an oath not to harm him, and she restores his men. This episode is significant because Circe, unlike Polyphemus, ultimately fulfils the obligations of xenia: she feeds, hosts and eventually helps Odysseus.

Circe is one of Homer’s most interesting characters. She begins the episode as a dangerous, magical predator who destroys men without warning. But once Odysseus resists her magic and confronts her directly, she transforms into a generous and knowledgeable host. She provides food, rest and, crucially, information: it is Circe who tells Odysseus he must travel to the Underworld to consult the dead prophet Teiresias before he can find his way home.

This transformation from threat to helper reveals something about Odysseus’s ability to bring order out of chaos through force of will and intelligence. It also raises the question of how Homer portrays powerful women. Circe has divine power, knowledge and authority that most of the male characters in the poem lack. Yet she ultimately places herself in service to Odysseus’s mission. The tension between her power and her submission to Odysseus reflects the poem’s broader interest in what makes a man truly dominant.

The Crew of Odysseus

In both episodes, the crew of Odysseus plays a crucial role — and not always a heroic one. In the Cyclops episode, it is one of Odysseus’s men who spots the cheese and lambs in Polyphemus’s cave and urges him to take them, rather than leaving as caution demanded. In Book 10, the crew’s curiosity and recklessness lead directly to their transformation into pigs. Homer’s point is consistent: Odysseus’s men lack their leader’s self-restraint and sophrosyne — the quality of knowing one’s limits. The men are brave and loyal, but they cannot resist the temptations placed in their way, and this failure will ultimately destroy them.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When analysing the Cyclops or Circe episodes, move beyond narrating what happens. The key question examiners are looking for is: what does this episode reveal about Odysseus’s character, about the poem’s themes, and about what Homer values? For a ‘source analysis’ question on a passage from Book 9 or 10, pick out specific details — a word, a phrase, an action — and say what it suggests about metis, xenia or the contrast between civilised and barbaric behaviour. For essay questions on the wanderings, a common error is to list all the adventures without ever arguing a point; instead, select two or three episodes, compare them, and build an argument.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • In Book 9, Odysseus escapes Polyphemus through metis (cunning): the Nobody trick, the sharpened stake and hiding under the rams. His boastful revelation of his name to the Cyclops sets Poseidon against him for the rest of the poem.
  • In Book 10, Circe transforms Odysseus’s men into pigs, but Odysseus — protected by the herb moly given by Hermes — resists and forces her to become his host; she ultimately helps him by directing him to the Underworld.
  • Both episodes contrast Odysseus’s disciplined intelligence with the recklessness of his crew, and both test the civilised value of xenia against characters who begin by violating it.

lessons.title: The Homecoming
lessons.description: Odysseus returns to Ithaca — the recognition scenes, the contest of the bow, and the slaughter of the suitors.
lessons.content_html:
The Return to Ithaca: Disguise and Deception

When Odysseus finally reaches Ithaca in Book 13, the goddess Athena disguises him as an old beggar. This disguise is essential to his plan: Ithaca is filled with over a hundred suitors who have taken over his palace, are consuming his wealth and are competing to marry his wife Penelope. If Odysseus is recognised too soon, he will be killed before he can prepare. The disguise is one of the most sustained and elaborate acts of deception in the poem, and it lasts through Books 13 to 22.

The theme of disguise and recognition is one of the Odyssey’s most powerful structural devices. Homer builds intense dramatic irony by allowing the audience to know what the characters in the poem do not: the ragged beggar shuffling through the halls of his own palace is the great king Odysseus. This gap between what the audience knows and what the suitors assume — that they are safe, that Odysseus is dead, that they may treat a helpless beggar with contempt — makes their eventual destruction feel both inevitable and just.

Book 19: Penelope and the Recognition by Eurycleia

In Book 19, still in his beggar’s disguise, Odysseus has a long, remarkable conversation with Penelope. She does not know she is speaking to her husband. She tells the “stranger” about her famous trick: she has been weaving a burial shroud for Odysseus’s father Laertes and has promised to choose a new husband when it is finished. Every night she unpicks the weaving she has done during the day, buying herself years of time. This deception is a mirror of Odysseus’s own resourcefulness — husband and wife are revealed to be perfectly matched in their use of cunning to protect what matters most to them.

The recognition scene that follows is both touching and tense. Penelope calls for the old nurse Eurycleia to wash the beggar’s feet — an act of hospitality appropriate for a guest. As Eurycleia washes his legs, her hands find a scar on his thigh. The poem pauses the action entirely to tell the story of how Odysseus received the scar as a young man, hunting a boar on Mount Parnassus with his grandfather Autolycus. This long digression — a retardation technique, not the anagnorisis itself — is a deliberate slowing of the pace that builds the dramatic tension almost unbearably. The anagnorisis comes immediately after: the moment Eurycleia’s hands find the scar and she realises the beggar is Odysseus.

Eurycleia gasps and looks up. Odysseus grabs her throat and silences her with a warning: no one must know. She agrees. This is the first human recognition in the palace, and it confirms for the audience what Odysseus has known all along — that there are loyal people in Ithaca waiting for his return, and that his plan can succeed.

Key Fact

Penelope’s weaving deception is her equivalent of Odysseus’s cunning: she weaves a shroud for Laertes by day and unpicks it by night, delaying her choice of a husband for years. The parallel between husband and wife — both using deception to hold off those who would take what is theirs — is one of Homer’s most deliberate structural echoes.

Book 21: The Contest of the Bow

In Book 21, Penelope announces a contest to decide who she will marry: any man who can string Odysseus’s great bow and shoot an arrow through the sockets of twelve axe-heads in a row may have her hand. The great bow of Odysseus, given to him long ago by the hero Iphitus, is an object of enormous symbolic importance. It is kept under lock and key and has not been used since he left for Troy. To string it requires enormous strength and skill — the kind that only its owner possesses.

One by one, the suitors try and fail to string the bow. The wood is seasoned and stiff; the string requires a technique that none of them can master. The contest grinds to a humiliating halt. Then Odysseus, still in his beggar’s disguise, asks to be allowed to try. The suitors mock him furiously. Penelope supports his right to attempt it. Odysseus strings the bow with casual ease — “as a skilled musician strings a lyre,” as Homer says in one of his most elegant extended similes — and shoots cleanly through all twelve axe-heads without rising from his stool.

The homecoming books contrast loyal and disloyal servants carefully. The swineherd Eumaeus and the cowherd Philoetius remain loyal to Odysseus throughout: they refuse to side with the suitors, treat the disguised beggar with xenia, and are entrusted with a role in the final battle. Eurycleia recognises Odysseus and keeps his secret.

In contrast, twelve maidservants have slept with the suitors and sided against Penelope. The goatherd Melanthius has actively helped the suitors and insults Odysseus even when disguised. After the slaughter of the suitors, these disloyal servants are punished: the maidservants are forced to clean up the bodies before being hanged in the courtyard, and Melanthius is mutilated. The poem’s treatment of these characters reflects a worldview in which loyalty to a rightful lord is a supreme virtue, and its betrayal demands the harshest punishment.

Book 22: The Slaughter of the Suitors

The moment after Odysseus strings the bow is the pivot of the whole poem. He turns, shoots the leading suitor Antinous through the throat, and announces himself: “You thought I would never come home from Troy. You have been wasting my household, violating my maidservants, and seeking to take my wife while I still lived. Dogs — you never feared the gods who rule the spacious heaven, or the anger of men to come. Your day of reckoning has arrived.” The battle that follows is swift and brutal. Odysseus and three loyal helpers — his son Telemachus, Eumaeus and Philoetius — kill all the suitors in the great hall.

The massacre is presented by Homer as an act of dike — justice — rather than mere revenge. The suitors have violated the sacred rules of xenia by abusing their host’s hospitality for years. They have dishonoured Penelope, threatened Telemachus and wasted Odysseus’s wealth. The gods, particularly Zeus, have sanctioned the punishment. Athena appears in the hall to tip the balance at a critical moment, showing that divine approval stamps the act as righteous.

Key Fact

The suitors are killed by Odysseus, Telemachus, Eumaeus and Philoetius in Book 22. Homer frames the slaughter as divinely sanctioned justice: the suitors violated xenia, threatened the rightful king’s household, and dishonoured the gods. Athena’s presence in the hall confirms divine approval.

The scale of the killing in Book 22 — over a hundred young noblemen murdered in the great hall — can shock modern readers. Homer is not naive about this: the families of the suitors object in Book 24 and Odysseus faces a further threat of civil war. Yet throughout the poem Homer has built a careful moral case. The suitors were repeatedly warned. The gods disapproved. Odysseus returned precisely in time to prevent Penelope being forced into a new marriage. The contest of the bow — Penelope’s idea, not Odysseus’s — gave the suitors every opportunity to redeem themselves if any had the strength to string the bow.

The poem’s final moral position is that the gods uphold justice, and that those who violate the sacred laws of xenia and respect for a rightful king will be punished. Odysseus is the instrument of that punishment. Whether readers find this satisfying or disturbing often depends on whether they share Homer’s worldview — and that difference of response is itself worth discussing in a good exam answer.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Books 19, 21 and 22 are rich with source analysis opportunities. For a ‘source analysis’ question, look for what specific details reveal: the scar passage in Book 19 reveals Odysseus’s past and uses the technique of digression to slow the pace at the crucial moment of recognition; the bow contest in Book 21 uses an extended simile (stringing the lyre) to signal Odysseus’s mastery. The biggest error students make in essay questions on the homecoming is failing to discuss what the events mean rather than what happens. Always connect the plot to a theme: recognition scenes test loyalty; the bow contest tests fitness to rule; the slaughter tests the poem’s concept of justice and xenia.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • In Book 19, Odysseus (disguised) talks with Penelope and is recognised by his nurse Eurycleia through a scar on his thigh; Homer uses a long digression about the scar’s origins to build tension at the moment of recognition.
  • In Book 21, Odysseus strings his own great bow with ease after all the suitors fail, signalling that the reckoning has come; the bow contest was devised by Penelope, not Odysseus, paralleling her husband’s own cunning.
  • In Book 22, Odysseus kills all the suitors with the help of Telemachus and two loyal servants; Homer frames this as divinely sanctioned justice against those who violated xenia and dishonoured a rightful king.

lessons.title: Odysseus the Hero
lessons.description: What makes Odysseus a hero — his qualities, flaws, and the Homeric heroic code of kleos, time and endurance.
lessons.content_html:
The Homeric Hero

In the world of the Odyssey, a hero is not simply a good person. A hero is someone who achieves great deeds, wins lasting fame, and earns the respect — and fear — of other men. The Homeric concept of heroism is built around two Greek values: kleos (glory) and time (honour). A hero’s kleos is the fame that survives his death, passed on in the songs of bards. His time is the honour shown to him by his community — gifts, prestige, the right to speak first at an assembly. To lose time is a devastating blow; to win kleos is the highest aspiration.

The Iliad, Homer’s other poem, presents the ideal of the warrior-hero most clearly in Achilles: the greatest fighter, whose wrath drives the whole story, who chooses a short glorious life over a long quiet one. Odysseus, by contrast, is a different kind of hero. He is brave and strong, but his defining virtue is intelligence, not brute strength. This creates a fascinating tension: is the cleverest man always the best hero? The Odyssey argues yes — and the prescribed books are Homer’s case for that argument.

Key Fact

Kleos (glory/fame) and time (honour) are the two central heroic values in Homeric epic. Kleos is the lasting fame a hero earns through great deeds — it lives on after death in poetry and song. Time is the immediate respect shown by a community. Losing either is a catastrophe; winning both is the ultimate aspiration.

Odysseus as Leader, Husband and Father

The Odyssey tests Odysseus’s heroism across three roles simultaneously. As a leader, he is responsible for the lives of his crew. He plans carefully, issues orders, and holds his men together in the face of terrifying obstacles. Yet his leadership is not always flawless: his men die, largely because they cannot match his self-restraint. In Book 12, they eat the sacred cattle of the sun god Helios, despite Odysseus’s explicit warnings. They are destroyed as a result. Odysseus’s failure as a leader is that he cannot always prevent his men from being their own worst enemy.

As a husband, Odysseus’s devotion to Penelope is the emotional core of the poem. He refuses the offer of immortality from the goddess Calypso, who holds him on her island for seven years, because he would rather be a mortal man with a wife and a home than an immortal without them. This choice is central to the poem’s values: Odysseus knows what he is and what he values. The home, the marriage bed, the kingdom — these are worth more to him than divine status.

As a father, his relationship with Telemachus is one of the poem’s most moving dimensions. Telemachus is twenty years old; he has grown up without a father. The poem traces his development from a boy who cannot challenge the suitors into a young man who fights alongside his father in Book 22. This growth is partly Athena’s work, but it is also inspired by Odysseus’s own example: when Telemachus sees what his father can do, he finds the courage to act.

Greek epic contrasts two kinds of heroic power. Bie (raw physical force) is the value of Achilles or Heracles — overwhelming strength that defeats enemies directly. Metis (cunning intelligence) is Odysseus’s value — the ability to solve a problem indirectly, through deception, disguise or verbal skill. The Odyssey is, in one sense, a sustained argument that metis is at least as valuable as bie — perhaps more so, since the challenges Odysseus faces cannot be defeated by strength alone.

The Cyclops episode is the clearest example. Polyphemus is vastly stronger than Odysseus and his men. Physical force would be useless. Only metis — the Nobody trick, the stake, the rams — can save them. Similarly, in Book 22 Odysseus does not defeat over a hundred suitors by physical prowess alone: he needs the element of surprise, a secured door, and the help of Athena. The poem suggests that a hero who knows when to use cunning and when to use strength is greater than one who can only do the latter.

The Flaws of Odysseus

Odysseus is not a perfect hero. His most prominent flaw, seen most clearly in the Cyclops episode, is excessive pride — what the Greeks called hubris. After escaping from Polyphemus, Odysseus cannot resist revealing his real name. The boast is humanly understandable — he has just achieved something extraordinary — but it is disastrous in its consequences, setting Poseidon against him for the rest of the poem. A truly wise hero would have stayed silent.

Odysseus also shows a capacity for ruthlessness that can disturb modern readers. He lies freely, to almost everyone he encounters. He shows very little grief for the men he loses. He kills the suitors without giving even the most innocent a chance to escape. Homer does not present these as straightforward virtues; the poem invites the reader to think hard about what kind of man Odysseus is, and whether his ends justify his means. This moral complexity is part of what makes the Odyssey worth studying.

Key Fact

Odysseus’s two most important flaws are pride (hubris — revealed by the boast to Polyphemus, which costs him Poseidon’s enmity) and his capacity for deception (he lies even to loyal characters, including Penelope in Book 19, though this is also what enables his survival). These flaws complicate his heroism without cancelling it.

One of the qualities Homer most praises in Odysseus is endurance — the ability to bear suffering without breaking. This is called karteria. Odysseus weeps for his home regularly, but he never gives up. He endures Calypso’s island for seven years without losing his sense of who he is. He sits in his own palace disguised as a beggar, being mocked and humiliated by the suitors, without revealing himself. This sustained self-control — knowing when to act and when to wait — is what ultimately wins him everything he wants.

This makes Odysseus a quite different kind of hero from Achilles, whose defining choice is to act immediately and violently when his honour is threatened. Odysseus chooses patience over pride (except in the Cyclops episode), strategy over impulse. Whether this makes him a more admirable figure than Achilles is a question the poem raises but does not simply answer — and that open question is ideal material for an essay.

Odysseus’s Relationship with Athena

Throughout the Odyssey, Athena is Odysseus’s protector and closest divine ally. She intervenes at almost every critical moment: she inspires Telemachus to seek news of his father, she engineers Odysseus’s release from Calypso’s island by appealing to Zeus, she gives Odysseus his beggar’s disguise, and she tips the balance of the battle in Book 22. Their relationship is explicitly described as a friendship of equals in intellect: Athena tells Odysseus that she favours him because he is “the cleverest of mortals,” just as she is the cleverest of the gods. This mutual recognition of metis — goddess and man bonded by their shared love of craft and cunning — is one of the most charming ideas in the poem.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions asking you to evaluate Odysseus as a hero, avoid simply listing his qualities. Examiners want to see you engage with the complexity: what are his strengths, what are his weaknesses, and how does Homer use specific episodes to reveal both? Always name the book and the episode (e.g. ‘in Book 9, his pride when he reveals his name to Polyphemus’). For essay questions that ask ‘how far do you agree,’ you must present both sides: the case that Odysseus is a great hero (metis, endurance, his relationships) and the case that his flaws undermine this (hubris, ruthlessness, the deaths of his crew). Reach a clear, supported conclusion — sitting on the fence is not a judgement.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Odysseus’s heroism rests on metis (cunning intelligence), karteria (endurance) and his devotion to kleos and time; he is defined by intelligence rather than strength, making him a different kind of hero from Achilles.
  • His key flaws are hubris (excessive pride, shown when he reveals his name to Polyphemus) and a capacity for ruthless deception; these complicate but do not cancel his heroic status.
  • Athena favours Odysseus precisely because he shares her defining quality — metis — and she intervenes at every critical moment to support his mission; his relationship with her is one of intellectual equals.

Against: his metis achieves what bie alone could not (Polyphemus, Circe, the suitors); his endurance (refusing Calypso's immortality, sitting as a beggar in his own hall) shows extraordinary self-control; his devotion to home over divine status is presented as admirable. A top answer will note that Homer does not resolve this tension simply — the poem invites the reader to hold the qualities and flaws simultaneously. Supported judgement required.

Developing: Mostly one side; limited evidence.
Emerging: General discussion of Odysseus without specific episodes.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between metis and bie as heroic values in the Odyssey, using specific examples from the prescribed books.
practice_questions.marks:

Bie: raw physical force (associated with Achilles in the Iliad; Polyphemus represents bie — massive but easily outwitted; the suitors' numerical strength is irrelevant against Odysseus's strategy). The key point is that the Odyssey argues metis is more valuable because the challenges of the homecoming cannot be solved by strength alone — only by intelligence, self-restraint and cunning.

lessons.title: Gods, Values & the Household
lessons.description: The gods, xenia, Penelope and Telemachus — the divine and domestic worlds that shape the Odyssey's meaning.
lessons.content_html:
The Role of the Gods in the Odyssey

The gods are not background figures in the Odyssey — they are active participants in the story, intervening at crucial moments to help or hinder the mortals they favour or resent. Homer opens the poem in a divine assembly: Zeus reflects that mortals blame the gods for their suffering, when in fact their own recklessness is usually the cause. This opening sets up the poem’s moral framework. The gods are not arbitrary or capricious in Homer’s version — they punish those who deserve it and reward those who honour them properly.

The two most important divine figures in the Odyssey stand in direct opposition to each other. Athena is Odysseus’s protector. She engineers his release from Calypso’s island by appealing to Zeus, guides Telemachus on his journey, gives Odysseus his beggar’s disguise, and intervenes in the battle of Book 22. Poseidon is Odysseus’s enemy. After Odysseus blinds his son Polyphemus, Poseidon does everything he can to prevent the homecoming — destroying ships, stranding the hero on distant islands, and stirring up deadly storms.

Key Fact

Athena (protector) and Poseidon (enemy) represent the two opposing divine forces in the Odyssey. The tension between them drives the structure of the poem: every time Poseidon obstructs Odysseus, Athena finds a way to help him forward. The poem suggests that Odysseus’s eventual success is divinely sanctioned — justice, as well as intelligence, is on his side.

Fate, Free Will and Divine Justice

A central question in the Odyssey is how much of what happens to characters is their own fault, and how much is the will of the gods. Zeus’s speech at the opening of the poem signals Homer’s position: mortals suffer when they act recklessly against divine warnings. Odysseus’s crew are warned not to eat the cattle of Helios; they eat them anyway and are destroyed. The suitors are given multiple warnings; they persist in their behaviour and are killed. Odysseus himself earns Poseidon’s enmity through his own pride.

Yet the gods are not neutral. Athena actively promotes Odysseus’s cause, and her intervention in Book 22 — appearing in the hall to tip the balance — shows that divine favour is not merely passive approval but direct action. The poem holds both ideas simultaneously: mortals are responsible for their own choices, and the gods shape the world those choices are made in. This is not a contradiction but a coherent worldview in which moral responsibility and divine authority coexist.

Xenia — guest-friendship — is arguably the most important value in the Odyssey. The code required a host to welcome any stranger with food and shelter before asking who they were or why they had come. It required guests to behave respectfully and not overstay their welcome. The whole system was protected by Zeus in his role as Zeus Xenios — protector of guests and strangers. Violation of xenia was a religious offence, not just a social one.

The poem is full of xenia encounters, and each one tests whether the code is being followed. The Phaeacians in Books 7 and 8 are model hosts: they entertain Odysseus lavishly, give him gifts, and eventually escort him home in their magical ships. The suitors in Ithaca are the counter-example: they have been “guests” in Odysseus’s hall for years, but they consume his wealth, harass his wife, threaten his son and abuse the real guests — most notably, the disguised Odysseus himself. Their violation of xenia is not just rude; it is impious. This is why their deaths are presented as divine justice rather than mere revenge.

Good Hosts and Bad Hosts in the Odyssey

One of the most consistent ways Homer builds his moral universe is by measuring each character and community against the standard of xenia. The contrast between good and bad hosts is a structural principle of the poem. Polyphemus is the worst possible host: he eats his guests instead of feeding them, dismisses the gods who protect xenia, and has no concept of the reciprocal obligation that defines civilised behaviour. The Phaeacians, by contrast, bring xenia to near-perfection: they ask no questions, provide lavish entertainment, allow Odysseus to tell his own story, and escort him home with gifts.

Circe begins as a hostile and dangerous host but is transformed by Odysseus’s resistance into a genuine one. She provides a year of hospitality, restores his crew, and gives him essential information. This progression — from failed xenia to fulfilled xenia — mirrors the arc of the whole poem: disorder being brought back to order, the world resetting around the proper code of behaviour.

Key Fact

The Phaeacians are the model hosts of the Odyssey: they entertain Odysseus without questions, hold games in his honour, allow him to narrate his adventures (Books 9–12), and eventually carry him home. This perfect xenia is deliberately contrasted with the suitors in Ithaca, who have turned the rules of hospitality entirely upside down.

Penelope: Host, Wife and Queen

Penelope is one of the most complex female characters in ancient literature. She is simultaneously a faithful wife (waiting twenty years for Odysseus), a resourceful strategist (the weaving trick, the bow contest), and a host who maintains the laws of xenia even under enormous pressure. When the disguised Odysseus arrives at the palace, it is Penelope who insists he be welcomed and treated according to the code — she orders Eurycleia to wash his feet and provides him with a bed, even as the suitors mock him.

Penelope’s intelligence mirrors Odysseus’s. The weaving trick shows she can use deception to protect what she values, just as Odysseus does. The bow contest in Book 21 is entirely her idea — Odysseus did not plan it. By setting the contest, she creates the mechanism for Odysseus’s revelation and the suitors’ destruction, though the poem is ambiguous about whether she consciously intends this or acts on instinct. This ambiguity makes her fascinating: she may be even more complicit in the plan than Homer openly states.

Telemachus begins the Odyssey as a boy unable to challenge the suitors. By Books 21 and 22, he stands beside his father and kills men in battle. His development — from passive youth to active hero — is one of the poem’s most carefully traced arcs. Athena appears to him in disguise at the start of the poem, encouraging him to seek news of his father and to start behaving like a prince. This divine push sets him on his journey.

Telemachus’s role in the homecoming is not merely that of a helper: he is Odysseus’s heir and the future of Ithaca. When Odysseus trusts him with the knowledge of his identity, it is because Telemachus has shown he is worthy. His willingness to fight alongside his father rather than hiding shows that the next generation of Ithaca’s ruling house is as capable as the last. The Odyssey is not just a story about one man returning home — it is about the restoration of a household and a dynasty.

Women and Men in the Homeric World

The Odyssey contains some of the most memorable female characters in ancient literature: Penelope, Circe, Calypso, the Phaeacian princess Nausicaa. This is not accidental. The poem’s central drama — the household of Ithaca under threat — is also a drama about the proper ordering of gender roles in Homer’s world. Penelope is celebrated precisely because she remains faithful and uses her intelligence in service of her husband’s return. Circe and Calypso are dangerous precisely because they represent the temptation to abandon that domestic world: Circe’s island (for a year) and Calypso’s (for seven years) are places where Odysseus forgets, temporarily, who he is. The poem consistently values homecoming over staying, and domestic loyalty over divine pleasure.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions about gods, values or characters in the Odyssey reward specificity. Do not say ‘the gods helped Odysseus’ — say ‘Athena appealed to Zeus in the divine assembly to secure Odysseus’s release from Calypso,’ and explain what this reveals about how divine patronage works in Homer. For xenia, name specific good and bad examples rather than making general statements. For Penelope, move beyond ‘she was loyal’ — explain the weaving trick as evidence of metis, and discuss the ambiguity around the bow contest. The best essay answers on values and character use two or three specific, well-chosen examples with developed analysis, rather than listing every character Homer ever depicts.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Athena (Odysseus’s protector) and Poseidon (his enemy) are the two main divine forces in the poem; their opposition shapes its structure, and Athena’s final intervention in Book 22 gives the homecoming divine sanction as an act of justice.
  • Xenia (guest-friendship) is the poem’s central moral standard: Polyphemus and the suitors violate it catastrophically; the Phaeacians embody it perfectly; every community Odysseus visits is measured against it.
  • Penelope and Telemachus are both active agents in Odysseus’s return: Penelope mirrors her husband’s cunning (the weaving trick, the bow contest) and Telemachus grows from passive boy to warrior, securing the future of the household.

practice_questions.text:
Read this paraphrase of a moment from the Odyssey:

'Athena appeared to Telemachus in the form of a stranger visiting the palace. She told him he had his father's eyes, and that she could see greatness in him. She urged him to call an assembly of the leading men of Ithaca, to challenge the suitors' presence in the hall, and then to set out on a journey to seek news of his father.'

What does this passage suggest about the role of the gods in the Odyssey, and about Telemachus as a character? Refer to specific details from the passage.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses at least two specific details with developed explanation. Likely points: Athena appears in disguise — the gods work indirectly in the Odyssey, using mortal appearance to nudge rather than command; 'she could see greatness in him' — divine recognition of heroic potential; the instructions (call an assembly, challenge the suitors, seek news of his father) show the gods actively shaping heroic development — Telemachus needs a divine push to act like a prince; 'she told him he had his father's eyes' — likening him to Odysseus signals his potential and links father and son thematically. The passage shows that divine intervention in the Odyssey is educative as well as practical.
Secure: Two details identified and explained.
Developing: One detail explained clearly.
Emerging: General comment on gods helping characters with little specific reference.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Homer presents Penelope as both a faithful wife and an intelligent strategist in the Odyssey.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: faithful wife — she waits twenty years for Odysseus to return, refusing to choose a husband even under enormous pressure. 1 mark for development: she maintains this faithfulness actively rather than passively (she controls the pace of events). 1 mark for: intelligent strategist — the weaving trick, unpicking her work each night, buys years of time. 1 mark for: the bow contest in Book 21 is Penelope's idea, which creates the mechanism for Odysseus's revelation and the suitors' destruction — this shows her intelligence may be as deliberate as her husband's.

practice_questions.text: 'Xenia is the most important value in the Odyssey.' How far do you agree? Refer to a range of episodes and give a supported judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained argument that engages with both sides. For xenia as central: it is the moral standard by which every community is judged (Polyphemus worst, Phaeacians best); the suitors' violation of xenia is the explicit justification for their deaths; Zeus as Zeus Xenios makes xenia a divine as well as social code; it structures the episodic narrative of the wanderings. Against: nostos (the drive home) is equally central — every temptation Odysseus faces is a test of whether his longing for home exceeds his desire to stay; metis (cunning) is the quality that actually determines survival; justice (dike) is the frame for the suitors' punishment. Top answers will argue that xenia and the other values are interlocking rather than competing — they form a coherent moral world together. Supported judgement required.
Secure: Two values compared with at least two episodes.
Developing: Mostly focused on xenia; limited comparison.
Emerging: General discussion of values without specific episodes.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Homer presents the relationship between Odysseus and his son Telemachus as important to the themes of the Odyssey.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed points with specific textual references. Points could include: the Telemachy (Books 1–4) sets Telemachus on a journey that mirrors his father's — both must overcome obstacles and prove themselves; Telemachus's development from passive to active hero is shown in his willingness to fight in Book 22; Odysseus trusts Telemachus with his secret identity before any other character except Eumaeus — this trust is evidence of Telemachus's proved worth; the father-son relationship restores the dynasty and the household, so its resolution is central to the poem's conclusion. The relationship also raises the theme of heroism as learnable — Telemachus becoming his father's worthy successor.
Secure: Two points with explanation.
Developing: One point developed; or two points without specific textual detail.
Emerging: General mention of Telemachus helping his father.
